aliases.name: Hantu Pusaka
aliases.meaning: Heirloom spirit, when inherited within a family lineage

description.summary: Hantu Raya ('Great Ghost') is a powerful Malay familiar spirit said to be bound to a human master — typically a bomoh (shaman) or pawang — for whom it serves as a strength-augmenting double. It demands strict ritual offerings and is inherited within families as hantu pusaka.
description.full: Hantu Raya, literally 'Great Ghost' or 'High Spirit', is one of the most powerful familiar spirits in Malay folklore and folk-Islamic practice. Unlike ordinary hantu, it is bound through pact to a human master — historically a bomoh (shaman) or pawang (specialist practitioner) — and serves as a supernatural double that performs labour, provides protection, and can act as an alibi for its master's whereabouts. Folktale descriptions give it a humanoid form covered in black hair save for the face, with rough grey skin, long sharp teeth, and red eyes; in service it most often takes on the appearance of its master. The pact requires regular offerings of ancak — a ritual meal traditionally consisting of yellow glutinous rice, eggs, roasted chicken, rice flakes, and a doll — failing which the spirit may turn on its master or its master's family. Hantu Raya is frequently inherited as hantu pusaka, descending through a lineage and binding successive generations to the offerings until it is ritually released. The figure is treated as problematic by orthodox Islamic authorities in Malaysia but persists strongly in popular belief and is a recurring presence in modern Malaysian horror cinema, most prominently the 2007 film Jangan Pandang Belakang and its 2009 sequel.

etymology.meaning: Literally 'Great Ghost' — denoting power, not necessarily kingship over other spirits.
etymology.first_use: Documented in 20th-century Malaysian ethnographies; full-scale academic treatment in Zain Tajudin's 1991 paper for the Journal of the Siam Society.

features.description: Folktale descriptions give Hantu Raya a humanoid form covered in black hair except on the face
Exposed facial skin described as rough and grey
Pronounced teeth in the natural form
When in service, takes on the exact appearance of its bound master

physical.morphology: Naturally a hairy humanoid; in operation, more often manifests as a perfect double of its master.

abilities.description: Manifests as a duplicate of its master, providing alibis and performing tasks in the master's place
Said to perform agricultural and other manual labour with strength beyond a human's
Some traditions hold that a Hantu Raya can direct or amplify the activity of lesser hantu
Cannot stray far from its base or master's home
Turns on the master or family if the ancak offering schedule is broken

behavior.diet: Ritual ancak offerings (yellow glutinous rice, eggs, roasted chicken, rice flakes, a doll)
patterns: Bound to a single human master through pact
Operates near the master's home (limited range)
Inherited as hantu pusaka within the master's lineage

range.description: Malay-Islamic cultural sphere of Maritime Southeast Asia: peninsular Malaysia in particular, with belief extending into Singapore, Brunei, southern Thailand, and parts of Indonesia.

first_recorded.source: Indigenous Malay folk religion; documented in 20th-century ethnographies

peak_activity_periods.description: Central role of bomoh/pawang and bound-spirit familiars in Malay village life
High-profile Malaysian horror cinema (Jangan Pandang Belakang, Jangan Pandang Belakang Congkak) brings Hantu Raya to mass audiences

temporal.seasonal_patterns: No strong seasonal pattern attested; tied to ritual calendar rather than season.

origins.cultural_roots: Pre-Islamic Malay animism, in which powerful nature- and ancestor-spirits could be bound through ritual pact, syncretized with Islamic notions of bound jinn under the bomoh/pawang tradition.
origins.earliest_accounts: Documented in modern Malaysian ethnography; substantial academic treatment in Haji Zain Tajudin's 1991 paper 'The Hantu Raya: A Malay Demon' in the Journal of the Siam Society.
origins.folklore_connections: Part of the Malay familiar-spirit complex alongside Pelesit, Polong, Toyol, Hantu Pusaka, and Bajang; distantly comparable to Western and Islamic figures of bound demonic familiars.

timeline.event: Haji Zain Tajudin publishes 'The Hantu Raya: A Malay Demon' in the Journal of the Siam Society (vol. 79, pt. 2)
timeline.significance: Major academic treatment of the figure

timeline.event: Jangan Pandang Belakang directed by Ahmad Idham released in Malaysia, prominently featuring Hantu Raya
timeline.significance: Popularizes Hantu Raya in modern mass-market Malaysian horror cinema

timeline.event: Jangan Pandang Belakang Congkak released as a sequel/spin-off
timeline.significance: Continued cinematic engagement with Hantu Raya as a curse passed through families

history.modern_era: Hantu Raya remains a recognizable figure in Malaysian popular culture and folk practice. Religious authorities discourage the practice of binding spirits, but folk belief in inherited Hantu Raya curses persists, especially in rural communities, and is recurrently dramatized in Malaysian horror media.

documentary.name: The Hantu Raya: A Malay Demon (Zain Tajudin, 1991)
documentary.description: Academic ethnographic article on the Hantu Raya in the Journal of the Siam Society.
documentary.analysis: Provides a structured ethnographic account of the figure, ritual practice, and folkloric range.

paranormal.name: Bound familiar / pact spirit
paranormal.description: Within Malay folk practice, Hantu Raya is a real spirit bound by oath to a human master in exchange for offerings, performing labour and protection.
evidence_cited: Reports of inherited curses through hantu pusaka

skeptical.name: Sociological function in village politics
skeptical.description: Folklorists and anthropologists read the Hantu Raya as encoding the social authority of the bomoh/pawang and the moral economy of ritual obligation in rural Malay villages.
evidence_cited: Hantu Raya stories used to explain prosperity, sudden misfortune, and intra-family conflict

skeptical.name: Theological objection (orthodox Islam)
skeptical.description: Mainstream Malaysian Islamic authorities consider the binding of spirits problematic or shirk-adjacent and discourage the practice while not necessarily denying the existence of jinn-like entities.

stories: A bomoh's Hantu Raya performing field labour in his exact form
A family cursed by an inherited Hantu Raya whose offerings have lapsed
A Hantu Raya turning against its master after broken pacts
folklore.beliefs: Belief in bound familiar spirits remains active in rural Malay-Islamic communities despite religious discouragement, and the inheritance pattern (hantu pusaka) is treated with serious caution.

indigenous.significance: A major figure in the Malay folk-Islamic spirit hierarchy and a key example of pre-Islamic / Islamic syncretism.
indigenous.sensitivity_note: Connected to living religious practice; should not be presented as fictional in contexts where the belief is current.
indigenous.respect_guidelines: Cite Malay-language and academic ethnographic sources. Distinguish folk practice from orthodox Islamic doctrine.
